about: WindLab's glossary (PRD UX-1). One source for the page's inline (?) definitions, the Glossary panel, the lessons and docs/GLOSSARY.md. Written for first-year engineering students: one plain sentence first, then a little more.

terms.short: The part of the air force on a body that acts at right angles to the wind.
terms.more: For a wing flying level, lift points up and holds the aircraft in the air. WindLab measures lift perpendicular to the wind direction, whatever the angle of attack.

terms.short: The part of the air force on a body that acts along the wind, holding the body back.
terms.more: Drag has two sources: pressure differences between the front and the back (pressure or form drag) and friction of the air rubbing along the surface (skin-friction drag). A finite wing adds induced drag.

terms.short: Lift divided by the dynamic pressure of the wind and the reference area: CL = L / (½ ρ V² S).
terms.more: Dividing by ½ρV²S removes the effect of size and speed, so CL describes the shape and its angle to the wind alone. A small aircraft wing cruises around CL 0.3 to 0.5; a wing section can reach about 1.5 before it stalls.

terms.short: Drag divided by the dynamic pressure of the wind and the reference area: CD = D / (½ ρ V² S).
terms.more: Lower is more streamlined. Using the frontal area, a sphere has CD about 0.47 and a modern car about 0.25 to 0.3; using the planform area, a wing at low angle has CD about 0.01 to 0.02. Always check which reference area a CD uses before comparing numbers.

terms.short: The nose-up or nose-down turning moment on the body divided by ½ ρ V² S and the reference length.
terms.more: WindLab takes the moment about the reference point, the quarter-chord of a built-in wing. Positive means nose up (the leading edge rises).

terms.short: Lift divided by drag, or CL divided by CD: how much lift you get for each unit of drag.
terms.more: Higher means more efficient. A glider reaches L/D of 40 or more; a small model wing in WindLab gives around 8 to 10. The angle with the best L/D is marked in a sweep.

terms.short: The angle between the wind and the body's reference line (for a wing, its chord line).
terms.more: In WindLab the part stays still and the wind is tilted: a positive angle means the wind comes from below, pushing the nose up. Lift grows roughly in proportion to the angle until the wing stalls.

terms.short: How much the lift coefficient rises for each degree of angle of attack.
terms.more: Thin-airfoil theory gives about 0.11 per degree for a 2D wing section. A real wing of finite span has a lower slope, the more so the smaller its aspect ratio: about 0.045 per degree for WindLab's default wing (aspect ratio 2).

terms.short: A pure number that compares the air's momentum with its stickiness: Re = V L / ν (speed × length ÷ kinematic viscosity).
terms.more: Flows with the same Reynolds number behave alike, whatever their size, which is why wind-tunnel models work. A 0.3 m chord at 20 m/s gives Re ≈ 410,000; an airliner wing flies at tens of millions. Below about a million the boundary layer stays laminar for a while, which lowers drag compared with WindLab's fully turbulent model.

terms.short: How sticky a fluid is: its resistance to being sheared.
terms.more: WindLab uses sea-level air at 15 °C with kinematic viscosity ν = 1.46 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s and density ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Viscosity is what makes a boundary layer form and what causes skin-friction drag.

terms.short: The pressure the moving air would exert if brought to a stop: q = ½ ρ V².
terms.more: At 20 m/s in sea-level air q ≈ 245 Pa. All the coefficients divide forces by q times a reference area, and the pressure coefficient divides pressure differences by q.

terms.short: The speed of the undisturbed air far from the part, in metres per second.
terms.more: 20 m/s is about 72 km/h. WindLab allows 1 to 100 m/s so the air can be treated as incompressible (Mach number below 0.3).

terms.short: The front-to-back length of a wing: the straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge.
terms.more: The chord is the reference length for a wing's Reynolds number and pitching moment. A tapered wing has a different chord at the root and the tip; WindLab then uses the mean aerodynamic chord.

terms.short: The tip-to-tip width of a wing, measured across the wind.
terms.more: Span times chord is the planform area of a rectangular wing. A longer span for the same area means a higher aspect ratio and less induced drag.

terms.short: How slender a wing is: span squared divided by planform area (span ÷ chord for a rectangular wing).
terms.more: Gliders have aspect ratios of 20 or more, fighter jets around 3. A higher aspect ratio gives a steeper lift slope and less induced drag; WindLab's default wing has aspect ratio 2.

terms.short: Tip chord divided by root chord: 1 for a rectangular wing, smaller for a wing that narrows towards the tips.
terms.more: Taper changes how lift is spread along the span and lowers the weight of a real wing.

terms.short: The area that CL and CD are divided by. For wings it is the planform area (chord × span); for cars and bluff bodies it is the frontal area.
terms.more: The choice is a convention, not physics: the same force gives a smaller coefficient with a larger area. WindLab's built-in wings use the planform area, the built-in bluff bodies their frontal area, and for an uploaded part it measures both from the surface and uses the frontal area for a body or the planform area for a wing-like part, unless you change it.

terms.short: The area of the body's silhouette seen from the front, straight into the wind.
terms.more: The usual reference area for bluff bodies and vehicles: a sphere of diameter d has frontal area π d²/4.

terms.short: The length used in the Reynolds number and the moment coefficient: the chord for a wing, the diameter or length for a body.
terms.more: WindLab also scales its virtual wind tunnel and mesh with the reference length, so a wrong value (for example from a units mistake) gives a wrong tunnel.

terms.short: The local pressure relative to the surrounding air, divided by the dynamic pressure: Cp = (p − p∞) / (½ ρ V²).
terms.more: Cp = 1 where the air is brought to a complete stop (the stagnation point at the nose), 0 where the pressure equals the surrounding air, and negative where the air speeds up and the pressure drops (suction, blue in WindLab's pictures). The suction on the upper surface of a wing is where most of its lift comes from.

terms.short: The spot on the front of a body where the oncoming air is brought to a stop and splits to flow around it.
terms.more: The pressure there is the highest on the body (Cp = 1). On a wing it sits just below the leading edge at positive angles of attack.

terms.short: Pressure below that of the surrounding air (negative pressure coefficient).
terms.more: Air that speeds up over a curved surface loses pressure, so it pulls on the surface rather than pushing. The suction peak near a wing's leading edge is where the pressure coefficient is most negative.

terms.short: A chart of lift coefficient against drag coefficient, one point per angle of attack.
terms.more: It shows how much drag each amount of lift costs. The point where a straight line from the origin just touches the curve has the best lift-to-drag ratio.

terms.short: A series of runs at several angles of attack on the same mesh: the classic wind-tunnel experiment.
terms.more: WindLab makes the mesh once and solves the flow once per angle, then draws CL against angle, the drag polar and L/D against angle.

terms.short: The loss of lift when the angle of attack is so large that the air can no longer follow the upper surface and separates from it.
terms.more: Lift stops rising and then drops while drag climbs steeply. WindLab's steady simulation predicts the linear range well but the stall angle and the lift after stall only roughly: the real flow there is unsteady.

terms.short: When the air stops hugging the surface and leaves it, forming a region of slow, swirling air (a wake).
terms.more: Separation happens where the pressure rises too quickly along the surface. Bluff bodies always separate and have a wide wake; a streamlined body delays separation to its tail and has a thin wake.

terms.short: The region of slowed, often swirling air behind a body.
terms.more: A wide wake means a lot of pressure drag: the pressure behind the body is low because the air cannot close in smoothly. In the flow slice it is the dark (slow) region downstream of the part.

terms.short: The thin layer of air next to a surface where the air is slowed down by friction, from zero speed at the wall to the full speed a little way out.
terms.more: It is a few millimetres thick on a model wing. Whether it is laminar (smooth) or turbulent (mixing) decides the skin friction and how easily the flow separates. WindLab assumes it is turbulent from the leading edge.

terms.short: Laminar flow moves in smooth layers; turbulent flow is full of random swirls that mix fast and slow air.
terms.more: A turbulent boundary layer has more skin friction but resists separation better. On a model at Re below about a million the boundary layer starts laminar and becomes turbulent part-way along (transition). WindLab assumes it is turbulent everywhere, which makes its drag at low Reynolds numbers higher than measured.

terms.short: The drag from the air rubbing along the surface inside the boundary layer.
terms.more: It is most of the drag of a streamlined body at low angle, and roughly doubles when the boundary layer turns from laminar to turbulent.

terms.short: The extra drag a finite wing pays for making lift: the tip vortices tilt the air downwards and so tilt the lift force backwards.
terms.more: It grows with the square of the lift coefficient and shrinks with aspect ratio: CDi ≈ CL² / (π e AR), with e about 0.9. This is why gliders have long, slender wings.

terms.short: The curvature of a wing section: how much its centre line bows upwards.
terms.more: A cambered section (NACA 2412) makes lift at zero angle of attack; a symmetric one (NACA 0012) makes none. Camber shifts the lift curve upwards without changing its slope much.

terms.short: A four-digit name for a classic family of wing sections: the first digit is the camber in percent of chord, the second where the camber peaks (in tenths of chord), the last two the thickness in percent.
terms.more: NACA 0012: symmetric, 12 % thick. NACA 2412: 2 % camber peaking at 40 % of the chord, 12 % thick. NACA was the US agency that became NASA.

terms.short: A body whose flow separates early, leaving a wide wake: a sphere, a cylinder, a flat plate, a cube, a lorry.
terms.more: Its drag is mostly pressure drag and its drag coefficient (on frontal area) is about 0.5 to 2, ten or more times that of a streamlined body of the same frontal area.

terms.short: A body shaped so the air can follow it all the way to a pointed tail: a teardrop, an airship, a wing section.
terms.more: Separation is delayed to the very back, the wake is thin, and the drag is mostly skin friction: a drag coefficient on frontal area of about 0.05 to 0.1, compared with 0.47 for a sphere.

terms.short: Length divided by maximum diameter of a streamlined body.
terms.more: Around 3 to 4 gives the least drag for a teardrop: slimmer bodies have more surface (friction), fatter ones more pressure drag.

terms.short: The division of the air around the part into hundreds of thousands of small cells; the solver computes the flow in each cell.
terms.more: Finer cells capture more detail but take longer. WindLab's Quick mesh has about 0.4 million cells, with thin layers along the surface for the boundary layer. Results depend a little on the mesh: see the expected-error ranges.

terms.short: The height of the first mesh cell at the wall, measured in the boundary layer's own units.
terms.more: y⁺ below 1 means the cell sits inside the thin laminar sublayer and the boundary layer is resolved; y⁺ of 30 to 300 means a wall function bridges the gap. WindLab's Quick mesh has y⁺ around 10 to 150 and uses a wall function; the 2D validation was wall-resolved.

terms.short: The path a particle of air follows through the flow; in a steady flow, the lines the air moves along.
terms.more: Streamlines bunch together where the air speeds up and spread out where it slows down. WindLab traces them in the mid-span slice; near the wing tips, where air also moves sideways, they are only a sketch.

terms.short: A cut through the air along the wind, through the middle of the part, coloured by air speed or pressure coefficient.
terms.more: It shows the stagnation at the nose, the fast air over the top of a wing and the wake behind. It is one plane of a 3D flow: what happens nearer the tips is different.

terms.short: The solver repeats its calculation (iterates) until lift and drag stop changing; then the result has settled, or converged.
terms.more: WindLab stops when CL and CD have been steady for at least a hundred iterations and the equations are satisfied closely enough. The 'wobble' is how much they still moved at the end: a measure of settling, not of accuracy. A result that did not settle is a rough guide only.

terms.short: The program that computes the airflow by solving the equations of fluid motion on the mesh: computational fluid dynamics (CFD).
terms.more: WindLab uses the open-source OpenFOAM solver in its steady, Reynolds-averaged form (RANS): it computes the average flow and models the effect of turbulence rather than following every swirl.

terms.short: The set of equations that stands in for the swirls the solver does not compute directly.
terms.more: k-ω SST is the usual choice for wings and vehicles. WindLab runs it fully turbulent: no laminar flow anywhere.

terms.short: The band next to a coefficient saying where the true value most likely lies, judged from WindLab's own validation runs.
terms.more: It comes from a small table built from comparisons with NASA's reference data and a mesh study. 'Unvalidated - treat as a trend only' means the shape, Reynolds number or angle is outside what was checked.

terms.short: A 3D file format that describes a surface as a list of triangles; every CAD program can export it.
terms.more: STL files carry no units, so WindLab asks which units the part was drawn in. The surface must be closed (watertight) to be meshed: export one solid body.

terms.short: The standard exchange format for exact CAD geometry (ISO 10303): SolidWorks exports it with File > Save As > STEP AP214.
terms.more: A STEP file keeps the true curved surfaces and says which units it uses, so WindLab can pre-select them; it still asks you to check the size. WindLab turns the surfaces into triangles itself (an STL) before meshing. Several bodies that touch are joined into one; separate bodies are an assembly, and WindLab uses the largest unless you ask for all.

terms.short: A surface with no holes: every triangle edge joins exactly one neighbour, so inside and outside are well defined.
terms.more: Only a watertight surface can be meshed. Surfaces exported as sheets, or several bodies touching along an edge, are not.

terms.short: WindLab works in metres; CAD parts are usually drawn in millimetres, so a part exported as '300' may be 300 mm or 300 m.
terms.more: A units mistake changes the Reynolds number by a factor of a thousand and the forces by a million. Check the size WindLab reports before running.

terms.short: WindLab's everyday mesh size: about 0.4 million cells, a run of one to five minutes on a laptop.
terms.more: Good for lift, trends and comparisons; its drag is a few percent to a third too high (see the expected-error ranges). Finer presets exist for later versions.

terms.short: A duct through which air is blown over a fixed model to measure the forces on it; WindLab is a virtual one computed on your laptop.
terms.more: WindLab's tunnel has no walls close to the part (20 reference lengths to the sides), so there is no blockage correction; its results compare with free-flight theory.

terms.short: A fast way to compute a flow on a grid of cells by letting packets of air hop between neighbouring cells and collide; WindLab's instant preview uses it in your browser.
terms.more: The preview is a 2D cut through the middle of the part at a Reynolds number of a few thousand (the full run is at hundreds of thousands), so it shows where the air speeds up, slows down and separates, but its lift and drag are only a rough sketch. Use the full simulation for numbers.
